text.text: Self-reported fitness instruments provide a scalable surveillance solution when objective testing is impractical, yet the nature of perception-accuracy discordance in adolescents is not well understood.

This study examined criterion-related validity, classification accuracy, convergent construct validity against the Spanish Perceived Physical Literacy Instrument (S-PPLI), and misclassification patterning of the International Fitness Scale (IFIS) in a community sample of adolescents from the Valle de Ricote (Region of Murcia, Spain).
Cross-sectional data from 1017 Spanish adolescents (471 boys, 546 girls; median age 14 years) from the Eating Healthy and Daily Life Activities (EHDLA) study were analyzed.

IFIS overall correlated with the Assessing the Levels of Physical Activity and Fitness (ALPHA-Fit) composite (Spearman rho [ρ] = 0.369; partial ρ = 0.377, p < 0.001), with flexibility showing the strongest domain-specific validity (Spearman ρ = 0.635; partial ρ = 0.592, p < 0.001).

text.text: Using the full five-level IFIS score, the area under the curve (AUC) for identifying the lowest fitness tertile was 0.66 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.63-0.69).

At the primary screening cut-off (IFIS ≤ 3), sensitivity was 0.68, specificity was 0.59, and negative predictive value was 0.80, while a stricter threshold (IFIS ≤ 2) increased specificity (0.94) at the cost of sensitivity (0.16).
Convergent validity with S-PPLI was supported (partial ρ = 0.56, p < 0.001).

text.text: Misclassification profiling identified 18.5% of participants as underestimators and 17.6% as overestimators; underestimation was associated with shorter sleep, while concordant-low membership was associated with higher body mass index (BMI), lower activity, and more sedentary time.
In conclusion, IFIS showed weak-tomodest criterion-related validity and limited discriminative accuracy.

Therefore, IFIS may serve as a lowburden adjunct to objective testing for population-level prioritization, but its performance relative to other brief instruments or low-burden measures, including BMI, remains untested.

The escalating prevalence of physical inactivity, coupled with rising adolescent obesity rates, 1, 2 and concurrent secular declines in cardiorespiratory and musculoskeletal fitness [3] [4] [5] [6] , constitutes a significant public health burden and is associated with increased risk of cardiometabolic disease and premature mortality. 7 With over 80% of school-aged adolescents failing to meet global physical activity (PA) guidelines, 8 there is a pressing need for scalable, low-cost surveillance instruments capable of efficiently identifying low-fitness individuals.

text.text: The International Fitness Scale (IFIS) was developed as a pragmatic self-report instrument to gauge perceived physical fitness (PF) in youth.

A systematic review and meta-analysis by Bao and colleagues, 9 with 13 studies (9634 participants), confirmed substantial test-retest reliability for the IFIS in children and adolescents, with pooled weighted kappa values of 0.724 to 0.764 across fitness domains.
text.formatted: A systematic review and meta-analysis by Bao and colleagues, <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">9</ref> with 13 studies (9634 participants), confirmed substantial test-retest reliability for the IFIS in children and adolescents, with pooled weighted kappa values of 0.724 to 0.764 across fitness domains.

text.text: However, this review was unable to pool validity estimates because primary studies reported heterogeneous methods and rarely reported standardized validity coefficients, and it identified only three studies that had formally assessed criterion validity.

Because it also documented marked between-study heterogeneity even for reliability (I² = 96.9-98.8%), the conditions under which IFIS responses are valid remain poorly characterized. 9 Sex is consistently associated with IFIS responses; girls systematically report lower perceived fitness than boys, a discrepancy that persists even when objective fitness levels are comparable. 10, 11 Whether this perceptual bias is associated with criterion-related validity or induces systematic misclassification has not been formally investigated.

text.text: While objective fitness testing constitutes the gold-standard reference, its widespread application is limited by logistical constraints, the necessity for trained assessors, and substantial demands on school curricula and time. 12, 13 Bao and colleagues 9 also documented a ceiling effect in youth samples, with most children and adolescents rating their fitness as good or very good and several studies collapsing response categories as a result.

text.text: Ceiling effects were directly consequential for screening, because they compressed the lower end of the response distribution and constrained the achievable sensitivity-specificity trade-off. 9 Still, ranking performance alone does not resolve a practical public-health question: whether IFIS can identify adolescents with low objectively measured fitness with acceptable classification performance.

text.text: Previous work has reported associations between low PF in adolescence and adverse health profiles. 14 Predictive validity reviews have confirmed associations between youth fitness and later cardiometabolic risk. 15, 16 Objective fitness indicators remain preferred reference standards.

text.text: However, studies often stop at correlation coefficients and do not examine screening metrics, likelihood ratios, or profile-level misclassification.
This limits direct translation to school surveillance and first-line clinical triage.
Consistent with this, the systematic review by Bao and colleagues 9 could not pool validity estimates and explicitly called for standardized reporting of validity coefficients in future studies.

text.text: We therefore aimed to assess criterion-related validity, classification accuracy, and misclassification patterning of IFIS against objective fitness components in a community sample of adolescents from Spain.
>Methods
text.formatted: <head n="2." >Methods</head>

text.text: Cross-sectional secondary analysis of the Eating Healthy and Daily Life Activities (EHDLA) study. 17 Ethical approval was obtained from the Bioethics Committee of Albacete (ID 2021-85, November 2021) and the Ethics Committee of Murcia (ID 2218/2018, February 2019).
text.formatted: Cross-sectional secondary analysis of the Eating Healthy and Daily Life Activities (EHDLA) study. <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">17</ref> Ethical approval was obtained from the Bioethics Committee of Albacete (ID 2021-85, November 2021) and the Ethics Committee of Murcia (ID 2218/2018, February 2019).

text.text: Written informed consent was obtained from parents/guardians and assent from participants.
Data were collected during the 2021-2022 academic year in three secondary schools in the Valle de Ricote (Region of Murcia, Spain) during physical education classes.
Adolescents aged 12-17 years were eligible; those with chronic conditions or exempted from physical education were excluded.

The sample size for the EHDLA study was calculated a priori using the formula n = (Z) 2 ) , assuming a 95% confidence level (Z = 1.96), an expected excess-weight prevalence of 40.0%, a 3% margin of error, and a 10% non-response rate.
This yielded a minimum required sample of 1138 adolescents.
However, for the present criterion-validity analysis, we used all participants with complete data for the prespecified IFIS validity workflow (n = 1017; 73.8% of the 1378 raw records).

No separate a priori power calculation was performed specifically for IFIS because this was a secondary analysis and the primary aim was estimation of validity and classification metrics rather than testing a single null hypothesis.

Nonetheless, the achieved sample provided adequate precision for the main estimates: the 95% confidence interval (CI) for the primary Spearman rho (ρ) correlation between IFIS overall and the objective composite was approximately 0.31-0.42, and the 95% CI for the primary area under the curve (AUC) was 0.63-0.69.

Missing data were not missing completely at random (MCAR) (chi-square [χ 2 ] test (499) = 740.1, p < 0.001) according to Little's test, 18 and complete-case analysis was used as described in Supplementary Note S1 and Table S1.

text.text: Self-reported fitness was captured with the IFIS, 10 covering overall fitness and four domain-specific items (cardiorespiratory, muscular, speed-agility, and flexibility) on five-point ordinal scales (1 = very poor to5 = very good; responses are stored as 0-4 in the EHDLA database and were recoded to 1-5 for analysis).

text.text: For binary screening analyses, low self-reported fitness was defined as IFIS overall ≤3 vs ≥ 4 (primary rule) and ≤2 vs ≥ 3 (stricter rule).
A sensitivity analysis examined the effect of collapsing the 'very poor' and 'poor' response categories.

All components were measured following the Assessing the Levels of Physical Activity and Fitness (ALPHA-Fit) 19 and expressed as sex-and age-specific z-scores: muscular composite (mean z-score of handgrip strength and standing long jump); speed-agility (reverse-coded 4 × 10 m shuttle run); flexibility (sit-and-reach); and cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF; 20 m multistage shuttle run).
text.formatted: All components were measured following the Assessing the Levels of Physical Activity and Fitness (ALPHA-Fit) <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">19</ref> and expressed as sex-and age-specific z-scores: muscular composite (mean z-score of handgrip strength and standing long jump); speed-agility (reverse-coded 4 × 10 m shuttle run); flexibility (sit-and-reach); and cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF; 20 m multistage shuttle run).

text.text: Participants for whom the 20 m shuttle run was not completed due to physical contraindications were excluded from CRF-specific analyses (n = 25).
For these participants, the objective fitness composite was computed as the mean of the three remaining component z-scores.
Z-scores were computed from sexand age-specific means and standard deviations in the EHDLA sample (internal reference), not from published external normative tables.

The sex-and age-specific median was chosen as the objective fitness threshold for profile definition because it yields approximately balanced high/low strata, maximizing statistical efficiency for cross-classifying perceived against objective fitness and avoiding the overrepresentation of concordant-low profiles that an extreme-tail definition would produce.
Tertile-and quartile-based definitions were retained for the primary classification accuracy analyses and for sensitivity analyses (Supplementary Note S2).
Body mass index (BMI) z-scores were computed with the World Health Organization growth references 20.

Waist-to-height ratio (WHtR) defined abdominal obesity. 21 Body fat percentage was estimated from triceps and medial calf skinfolds using Slaughter equations. 22 Resting blood pressure (BP) was averaged from two seated measurements; elevated BP (high-normal BP or hypertension) was defined by European Society of Hypertension age-, sex-, and height-specific categories. 23 PA and sedentary behavior were assessed with the Spanish Youth Activity Profile (YAP-S). 24 Sleep duration was derived from weekday and weekend bed/wake times.

text.text: Convergent construct validity was additionally assessed against the Spanish Perceived Physical Literacy Instrument for adolescents (S-PPLI; 9-item short form), previously validated in Spanish adolescents. 25

text.text: Criterion-related validity was examined via Spearman correlations and sex-and age-adjusted partial Spearman correlations, with linear trend contrasts modeled using ordinary least squares (OLS) regression with heteroskedasticity-consistent (HC0) standard errors.

Classification accuracy was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves, AUC with bootstrap 95% CIs (3000 resamples, percentile method), sensitivity, specificity, positive and negative predictive values (PPV/NPV), and positive and negative likelihood ratios (LR+/LR-). 26 For all ROC and AUC analyses, the full five-level ordinal IFIS response (1 = very poor to5 = very good) was used as the predictor; IFIS was not dichotomized for AUC estimation.
text.formatted: Classification accuracy was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves, AUC with bootstrap 95% CIs (3000 resamples, percentile method), sensitivity, specificity, positive and negative predictive values (PPV/NPV), and positive and negative likelihood ratios (LR+/LR-). <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">26</ref> For all ROC and AUC analyses, the full five-level ordinal IFIS response (1 = very poor to5 = very good) was used as the predictor; IFIS was not dichotomized for AUC estimation.

text.text: The binary IFIS rules (IFIS ≤ 3 vs ≥ 4 and IFIS ≤ 2 vs ≥ 3) were applied only to define screen-positive status and to compute threshold-specific operating characteristics (sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, LR+ and LR-).
Thus, AUC reflects the discriminative capacity of the full IFIS scale, whereas the threshold-specific metrics describe performance at the prespecified cut-off.
The same approach was used for domain-specific analyses, using the full five-level response of the corresponding IFIS domain item.
Differences between domain-specific AUCs were tested by paired bootstrap (2000 resamples).

Secondary construct validity used OLS regression (HC0 standard errors) for continuous adiposity and BP outcomes and robust Poisson regression with sandwich variance for binary outcomes (prevalence ratios [PRs]).

Misclassification profiles were defined by cross-classifying IFIS ≥ 4 (good or very good) vs ≤ 3 (average, poor, or very poor) against objective fitness at or above vs below the sex-age median composite, yielding four groups: concordant low, overestimators, underestimators, and concordant high.
Profile membership was modeled with robust Poisson regression (each profile vs all others), with BMI z-score as the primary adiposity predictor; WHtR was excluded due to collinearity.

Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (BH-FDR) correction was applied across the 24 simultaneous tests of the profile models, and separately across the four χ 2 tests of profile distribution (q < 0.05). 27 All analyses were conducted in Python (version 3.13.7) using pandas, NumPy, SciPy, statsmodels, and scikit-learn.

text.text: The analytical sample comprised 1017 adolescents (471 boys, 546 girls; median age 14 years, interquartile range [IQR] 13-15).

text.text: For the primary low-fitness definition (lowest sex-age tertile), the AUC based on the full five-level IFIS overall score was 0.66 (95% CI 0.63-0.69).
At the primary binary threshold (IFIS ≤ 3 vs ≥ 4), sensitivity was 0.68, specificity was 0.59, PPV was 0.44, NPV was 0.80, LR+ was 1.67, and LR-was 0.54.
The stricter threshold (IFIS ≤ 2 vs ≥ 3) reduced sensitivity to 0.16 while increasing specificity to 0.94 (LR+ = 2.45, LR-= 0.90).
Across secondary low-fitness definitions, AUC ranged from 0.64 to 0.67, and at the primary rule sensitivity (0.64-0.69) and specificity (0.57-0.64) remained moderate across all definitions.

Domain-specific AUC ranked as: flexibility 0.75 (95% CI 0.71-0.78), speed-agility 0.69 (95% CI 0.65-0.72), overall 0.66 (95% CI 0.63-0.69), CRF 0.65 (95% CI 0.62-0.69), and muscular fitness 0.64 (95% CI 0.61-0.67; Table 4, Fig. 1).

text.text: This analysis extends IFIS evidence by incorporating classification accuracy metrics and a systematic misclassification profiling framework.

IFIS demonstrated weak-to-modest criterion-related validity (partial ρ = 0.377) and limited screening utility for low objective fitness (AUC = 0.66), consistent with prior validation work in European and Latin American cohorts. 10, 11 The systematic review by Bao and colleagues 9 was unable to pool criterion-validity estimates owing to methodological heterogeneity, and our findings help illustrate why: the present estimates (partial ρ = 0.377; AUC = 0.66) would be difficult to combine with studies reporting only narrative validity results or unstandardized coefficients.

text.text: Additionally, likelihood ratios close in the minimal range indicate limited informativeness: at the primary threshold (IFIS ≤ 3 vs ≥ 4), sensitivity was 0.68 and specificity 0.59, with an LR+ of 1.67 and an LR-of 0.54, both in the range conventionally regarded as minimal.
These findings do not support describing IFIS as a useful screening or surveillance instrument in the conventional sense.

An AUC below the conventional threshold for acceptable discrimination and likelihood ratios of this magnitude collectively indicate that the instrument cannot reliably distinguish adolescents with low objective fitness from those without.

The NPV of 0.80 should be interpreted in light of the prevalence of low objective fitness under the tertile definition (322/1017, 31.7%), because NPV depends on prevalence as well as on sensitivity and specificity: a negative screen lowered the probability of low objective fitness from 31.7% to 19.9%, whereas a positive screen raised it to 43.7%.
Neither result is therefore decisive for an individual adolescent.

The stricter threshold (IFIS ≤ 2 vs ≥ 3) flagged only 9.2% of adolescents and was highly specific (0.94) but missed most adolescents with low objective fitness (sensitivity 0.16; LR+ 2.45), so it may be preferable only when minimizing false positives is the overriding priority.

Threshold selection should therefore follow the surveillance objective: the primary rule offers a balanced but modest operating point for population-level prioritization, whereas the stricter rule identifies a small, more selected group.
Neither threshold, however, supports confident individual-level classification.

IFIS is best regarded as a prioritization tool for population surveillance, and only relative to objective testing since its performance against other low-burden instruments remains untested, rather than a substitute for objective fitness testing in individual-level decisions.
An important interpretive caveat is that this study did not perform a head-to-head comparison of IFIS against other low-burden tools or against BMI as competing screening measures.

BMI z-score and other adiposity indicators were available in EHDLA and were analyzed as construct-validity correlates and as predictors of perception-accuracy profiles, 17 but they were not evaluated against the same objective fitness reference standard using identical classification-accuracy metrics.

text.text: Consequently, the present findings support conclusions about the absolute validity and classification performance of IFIS only; they do not establish whether IFIS performs better or worse than BMI or any other brief self-report instrument for identifying adolescents with low objective fitness.
Comparative validation against alternative low-burden measures is needed before any claim of relative utility can be made.
The distribution of IFIS responses is closely tied to these metrics and warrants explicit interpretation.
Although AUC is prevalence-and threshold-independent, the operating characteristics at any given cut point are constrained by the distribution of the predictor.

Because responses were concentrated in the average and good categories (801/ 1017, 78.8% combined), the primary rule split the sample approximately in half (49.6% screen-positive) and yielded a balanced but modest operating point, whereas only 94/1017 (9.2%) of adolescents rated their fitness as poor or very poor, which mechanically limited the sensitivity of the stricter rule.

The distribution of IFIS responses in our sample also differs from the pattern documented in the systematic review by Bao and colleagues. 9 They reported a ceiling effect in youth samples, with most children and adolescents rating their fitness as good or very good, and four included studies collapsed response categories to mitigate it.

text.text: In the present sample, the ceiling effect was less pronounced: half of the participants (50.4%) rated their overall fitness as good or very good, only 12.0% chose very good.
Two non-exclusive explanations are plausible.

First, the EHDLA cohort was drawn from a rural municipality with a high documented prevalence of excess weight, which may correspond to genuinely lower fitness and lower perceived fitness. 17 Second, the sex composition of the sample (54% girls) and the lower ratings observed among girls may have shifted the pooled distribution downward.

text.text: Whatever the explanation, the contrast is consequential for screening: the same cut-off can yield very different screen-positive rates, sensitivity, and specificity depending on where responses are concentrated, and the scarcity of poor and very poor ratings here limits the usefulness of stricter cut-offs.
This underscores that the operating characteristics of IFIS are not fixed properties of the instrument but depend on the distribution of responses in the population to which it is applied.
Domain-specific discrimination was heterogeneous.
Flexibility yielded a significantly superior AUC (0.75 vs 0.66 overall, p < 0.001), while muscular fitness showed the lowest discrimination (0.64).

text.text: This gradient likely reflects differential accuracy of self-perception by domain, and several non-mutually exclusive mechanisms may help explain it.

CRF, muscular strength/power, and speed-agility are typically revealed only under maximal, effortful, and infrequent testing conditions (shuttle runs, dynamometry, sprints), so self-assessment may rely on recalling a discrete past performance. 28 Flexibility, by contrast, is experienced continuously and submaximally in ordinary movement (reaching, bending, twisting), which may provide adolescents more frequent low-effort opportunities to calibrate their self-assessment against real joint range-of-motion feedback. 28, 29 Flexibility is also less socially salient and less tied to athletic identity or competitive comparison than muscular strength or speed-agility, which may be associated with weaker influence of self-presentational bias and gender-typed expectations, 30 and it may be less confounded by pubertal timing and body-composition changes, which may reduce maturational noise in self-perception. 28, 30 Conversely, the lowest AUC for muscular fitness may reflect greater susceptibility of perceived muscular capacity to social comparison, body-image concerns, and variability in perceived exertion. 28 These interpretations align with the broader literature on physical self-perception but remain partly speculative because body image, athletic competence, and perceived exertion were not directly measured in the present study.

text.text: In addition, the systematic review by Bao and colleagues 9 reported that criterion validity has been formally assessed in only three studies, and none has compared domain-specific classification accuracy; the flexibility advantage observed in our study should therefore be regarded as a novel finding requiring replication.

text.text: From a surveillance perspective, the observed gradient supports reporting domain-specific IFIS items separately, with the flexibility item carrying the greatest informational value for flexibility-specific low fitness.

Because each domain item was validated against its own domain-matched objective test, these results do not establish that any single item, including flexibility, can serve as a proxy for overall fitness.
Beyond their psychometric interest, the domain-specific results carry three direct operational implications for school-based and public health surveillance.

First, when domain-specific low fitness is the surveillance target, the flexibility item showed the highest domain-matched accuracy of all IFIS items, given its significantly higher AUC (0.75 vs 0.66) and stronger criterion correlation (partial ρ = 0.592).
However, this advantage pertains to flexibility itself and should not be interpreted as evidence that the flexibility item indexes overall fitness.
When a global low-fitness flag is required, the overall IFIS score remains preferable, as it was the only item validated here against the composite objective fitness criterion.
Second, domain-level responses should be inspected separately rather than collapsed into a composite, since the composite masks marked heterogeneity in perceptual accuracy across domains.
Third, there is a notable mismatch between measurement burden and self-report accuracy.
CRF is the most burdensome domain to assess objectively yet not the most accurately perceived, whereas flexibility is both the most accurately perceived and the least burdensome to measure.

Taken together, these findings are consistent with, but do not directly test, a two-stage approach in which a brief self-report screening tool is used to identify individuals who may benefit from objective assessment, followed by confirmatory field testing among those who screen positive.
Such an approach would preserve the role of objective testing in individual-level decision-making while potentially allowing its more targeted use.

However, because no two-stage algorithm was evaluated in the present study, its efficiency, cost-effectiveness, and incremental value over universal objective testing remain to be established in implementation research.
Domain-specific responses may also support tailored feedback, although this remains a hypothesis for intervention research.
Misclassification was frequent (36.1%) and bidirectional, with similar proportions of underestimators (18.5%) and overestimators (17.6%).

Girls rated their overall fitness lower than boys despite similar objective fitness (Table 1), a well-documented pattern 10 linked to physical self-concept, body image, and sociocultural norms 31 although these constructs were not directly measured in the present study and such explanations therefore remain speculative.

text.text: Even so, the distribution of profiles did not differ by sex (p = 0.160).

Additionally, because the objective composite was z-score based within the EHDLA distribution, many participants with average fitness could be classified as objectively non-low-fit while perceiving themselves as below average relative to social comparison standards.

In practice, a program relying on self-reported low fitness at the primary threshold would identify about two-thirds of truly low-fit adolescents (sensitivity 0.68) while also flagging 41% of those without low objective fitness (284/695).

Following correction for multiple comparisons, concordant-low membership was associated with higher BMI z-score, lower PA, and greater sedentary behavior, and concordant-high membership showed the mirror-image profile.

These characteristics align with the broader behavioral and anthropometric profile typically observed among adolescents with lower levels of PF, who tend to exhibit higher adiposity and lower engagement in PA. 32, 33 Underestimator membership was inversely associated with sleep duration, whereas its nominal association with BMI z-score did not survive correction.

text.text: However, this interpretation is speculative in the absence of actigraphy or perceived exertion data, and the modest strength of this association (PR 0.84; q = 0.033) warrants caution.
No characteristic was associated with overestimator membership after correction.
The construct-validity gradients between IFIS overall and adiposity, WHtR, body fat percentage, and systolic BP converge with the broader adolescent fitness literature 14, 21, [35] [36] [37] .

text.text: The practical implication is a caution rather than an endorsement.

Where self-reported fitness is used in surveillance, it should be understood as generating a screen-positive group within which objective fitness varies widely (PPV 0.44) and a screen-negative group that still includes about one in five adolescents with low objective fitness.
Surveillance systems that treat a positive IFIS response as indicating low fitness would likely misclassify a substantial proportion of adolescents.

Convergent associations with S-PPLI are consistent with IFIS capturing related but non-identical self-perceived constructs, with the strongest overlap for self-confidence and more modest alignment for communication and knowledge domains.

This pattern is consistent with IFIS indexing perceived PF rather than the broader multidimensional construct of perceived physical literacy, and it supports construct validity without implying interchangeability between instruments.

Strengths include sex-age standardization, domain-specific IFIS analyses, multiple low-fitness thresholds, Wilson score CIs for all binary proportion metrics, FDR correction for multiple comparisons, and a dedicated misclassification model.
Several limitations should be considered when interpreting these findings.

First, the cross-sectional design precludes causal inference and prevents assessment of whether perception-accuracy profiles are temporally stable or predictive of subsequent cardiometabolic trajectories.
Second, the complete-case analytical sample was confirmed by Little's test to be non-MCAR, indicating that excluded participants were not randomly distributed across the variable space.

Although the direction and likely magnitude of the resulting selection bias cannot be established without the missing values, findings may not generalize to adolescents who more frequently present with incomplete covariate profiles.
Third, the EHDLA study was powered to estimate excess-weight prevalence, this secondary analysis was not specifically powered for IFIS criterion validity or classification accuracy.
However, the 95% CIs for the main validity and screening estimates were sufficiently narrow to support the reported inferences.
Fourth, the sample was drawn from a single rural municipality in Spain, and ALPHA-Fit z-scores were standardized to the internal EHDLA distribution rather than external normative references.
This restricts generalizability to other adolescent populations and limits comparability of absolute fitness levels with studies using external norms.
As noted above, no head-to-head comparison with BMI or other low-burden instruments was performed, so no relative-utility claim is made.
Fifth, as discussed above, the distribution of IFIS responses constrained the operating characteristics achievable at each threshold.
The AUC of 0.66 should therefore not be interpreted as uniformly modest discrimination across the ROC curve.
Relatedly, no IFIS threshold provided decisive individual-level classification.
At the primary threshold, the LR-of 0.54 falls in the minimal range, meaning that a negative screen reduces but does not eliminate the probability of low objective fitness.
The instrument cannot rule out low fitness with confidence in an individual adolescent; its value lies in ranking and prioritization at the population level.

Because the ceiling effect in this sample was less pronounced than that documented in a systematic review, 9 the operating characteristics reported here have limited comparability with samples in which most adolescents rate their fitness as good or very good.

text.text: Sixth, pubertal stage was not assessed and could not be adjusted for in any model.

This is a substantive gap in an adolescent sample: puberty is characterized by rapid, sex-divergent changes in body composition, muscular strength, and physical self-concept, and adolescents at different maturational stages may perceive the same objective fitness level very differently. 38 Residual confounding by pubertal timing therefore remains plausible and may contribute to the sex differences in IFIS ratings and perception-accuracy group membership.

text.text: Seventh, psychosocial determinants of fitness self-perception (such as: body image dissatisfaction, perceived athletic competence, prior sport participation history, and socioeconomic position) were not evaluated, limiting the explanatory completeness of the profile-membership models.

Eighth, the mechanisms proposed to explain the domain-specific gradient in classification accuracy (particularly the greater accuracy for flexibility) were not directly tested because perceived exertion, body image, athletic competence, and sport participation history were not measured.
These explanations should therefore be regarded as hypothesis-generating.

Finally, WHtR was excluded from the Poisson profile models due to collinearity with BMI z-score and quasi-complete separation in the smaller profile subgroups, constraining the adiposity indicators available for profile characterization to a single composite measure.

Future studies should specifically test whether discrepancy-profile assignment at baseline is associated with differential responsiveness to fitness interventions (for example, whether underestimators may respond differently to motivational framing than concordant-low adolescents who face genuine fitness deficits).

Longitudinal and multicenter designs spanning diverse geographic, cultural, and socioeconomic contexts are also needed to establish whether perceptionaccuracy profiles are temporally stable, generalizable beyond singlesite rural samples, and predictive of longer-term cardiometabolic health trajectories.
Replication in cohorts with direct measures of physical self-concept, body image, and pubertal stage would allow the explanatory mechanisms proposed here to be formally tested rather than inferred.

In this single-region sample of adolescents from the Valle de Ricote (Region of Murcia, Spain), IFIS demonstrates weak-to-modest criterionrelated validity and limited discriminative accuracy for low objectively measured fitness, with the flexibility item showing the strongest domain-matched validity.
This domain-specific advantage should not be extrapolated to overall fitness, and the overall score remains the more appropriate global indicator.
At the primary threshold, sensitivity and specificity were both moderate, so that neither a positive nor a negative screen was decisive for an individual adolescent.

Misclassification was frequent, bidirectional, and associated with adiposity and lifestyle characteristics after correction for multiple comparisons, supporting integration of perception-accuracy profiling into adolescent surveillance rather than its immediate adoption.

Because the discriminative accuracy of IFIS was modest and established only relative to objective testing, and because no threshold examined provided confident individual-level classification, objective fitness testing remains the reference standard for individual-level decisions.
